questions.stem: A real symmetric matrix A is positive definite if xᵀAx>0 for every non-zero real vector x. Which statement about its eigenvalues is necessarily true?
options: At least one eigenvalue must be zero
explanations: Correct. For a real symmetric matrix, positive definiteness is equivalent to all eigenvalues being strictly positive.
Non-positive eigenvalues would violate xᵀAx>0 for an eigenvector associated with such an eigenvalue.
A zero eigenvalue would make the quadratic form zero for a non-zero eigenvector, contradicting positive definiteness.
Real symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues by the spectral theorem.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Set Theory & Algebra; Linear Algebra; standard spectral theorem and positive-definite matrices, e.g. Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right.

questions.subtopic: Cyclomatic number of a connected graph
questions.stem: A connected undirected graph has 8 vertices and 10 edges. What is its cyclomatic number, i.e. the number of independent cycles?
explanations: A connected graph with 8 vertices needs 7 edges for a spanning tree, so one extra edge would be one independent cycle, not one here.
Two independent cycles would require 9 edges for 8 vertices.
Correct. For a connected graph, the cycle rank is E−V+1=10−8+1=3.
Four independent cycles would require 11 edges for 8 vertices.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Combinatorics and Discrete Structures; Graph Theory; Rosen, Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications, cycle rank of a graph.

questions.subtopic: Cayley's formula for spanning trees of a complete graph
questions.stem: How many distinct spanning trees does the complete graph K₄ contain?
explanations: K₄ has more than eight spanning trees.
Twelve is not the value given by Cayley's formula.
Correct. Cayley's formula states that Kₙ has nⁿ⁻² spanning trees; for n=4, 4²=16.
Twenty-four is 4!, which counts vertex permutations, not spanning trees.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Combinatorics and Discrete Structures; Graph Theory; Cayley's formula, standard graph-theory result.

questions.stem: Which condition is equivalent to an undirected graph being bipartite?
options: It contains at least one Hamiltonian cycle
It contains no cycle of any length
It contains no cycle of odd length
explanations: A bipartite graph need not contain a Hamiltonian cycle.
A bipartite graph may contain even cycles, so it need not be acyclic.
Correct. An undirected graph is bipartite if and only if it has no odd cycle.
Even degrees at all vertices do not guarantee bipartiteness; for example, K₃ has all degrees 2 but is not bipartite.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Combinatorics and Discrete Structures; Graph Theory; standard characterisation of bipartite graphs, e.g. West, Introduction to Graph Theory.

questions.subtopic: Negation of a universally quantified implication
questions.stem: What is the logically equivalent negation of the statement ∀x(P(x)→Q(x))?
explanations: The negation of a universal statement is existential, not universal.
Correct. Negating P→Q gives P∧¬Q; negating the universal quantifier gives an existential counterexample.
This expression is equivalent to the original implication after quantifier transformation, not its negation.
This is not the logical negation of the original universally quantified implication.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Combinatorics and Discrete Structures; Mathematical Logic; Rosen, Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications, predicate logic and quantifier negation.

questions.subtopic: Sequential circuit timing: minimum clock period
questions.stem: A register-to-register path has clock-to-Q delay 0.6 ns, combinational delay 2.1 ns and setup time 0.3 ns. Ignoring skew and uncertainty, what is the minimum clock period required for correct capture?
explanations: 2.1 ns omits both the launch register's clock-to-Q delay and the capture register's setup requirement.
2.7 ns includes clock-to-Q and combinational delay but omits setup time.
Correct. The minimum period is tCQ + tcomb + tsetup = 0.6 + 2.1 + 0.3 = 3.0 ns.
3.6 ns adds an extra 0.6 ns not required by the stated path model.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Digital Logic; sequential-circuit timing and setup constraints; Mano, Digital Design, sequential circuit timing.

questions.stem: In 8-bit signed two's-complement arithmetic, the bit patterns for +100 and +60 are added. What result is stored, and what is the status of the operation?
explanations: Correct. 100+60=160; modulo 256 the stored byte is 1010 0000, which represents −96 in 8-bit two's complement. Since two positive operands produce a negative result, signed overflow occurred.
+160 is outside the representable range −128 to +127, so it cannot be represented without overflow in 8 bits.
The stored pattern represents −96, but the operation does overflow because the mathematical result is outside the signed range.
+32 is not the modulo-256 sum of the two operands.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Digital Logic; number representation and computer arithmetic; Mano, Computer System Architecture, signed binary arithmetic.

questions.stem: Two valid packed-BCD digits, 8 and 7, are added. After the required BCD correction, what packed-BCD result represents the decimal sum?
explanations: 0000 1111 is the uncorrected binary sum 15, not a valid single BCD digit representation.
Correct. 8+7=15; the BCD result is tens digit 0001 and units digit 0101, i.e. 0001 0101.
0001 0001 represents decimal 11 in packed BCD.
0000 1001 represents decimal 9, not 15.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Digital Logic; computer arithmetic and BCD addition; Mano, Digital Design, number codes and arithmetic circuits.

questions.stem: A 4-to-1 multiplexer uses A as the most significant select input and B as the least significant select input. Which data-input assignment implements F=A⊕B?
explanations: Correct. For select AB=00,01,10,11, XOR outputs 0,1,1,0 respectively, so the four data inputs must match that sequence.
This assignment implements XNOR, the complement of XOR.
This assignment produces F=A, not XOR.
This assignment produces F=¬A, not XOR.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Digital Logic; combinational circuit synthesis using multiplexers; Mano, Digital Design, multiplexers and Boolean functions.

questions.stem: A byte-addressable 32-bit machine has a 32 KiB, two-way set-associative cache with 64-byte blocks. Assuming conventional indexing, how many tag bits are in a physical address?
explanations: Sixteen bits would leave too many bits assigned to the set index or block offset.
Correct. There are 32 KiB/64 B=512 blocks and 512/2=256 sets, so offset=6 bits, index=8 bits and tag=32−6−8=18 bits.
Twenty bits would result from using an incorrect smaller index or offset field.
Twenty-two bits would undercount the number of address bits needed for the set and byte offset.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Computer Organization and Architecture; cache organisation and address fields; Patterson and Hennessy, Computer Organization and Design, cache mapping.

questions.stem: An ideal five-stage pipeline has a one-cycle stage latency and no stalls. How many clock cycles are required to complete 100 instructions after the pipeline is filled?
explanations: 100 cycles would be the ideal count only if the pipeline had one stage.
Correct. An ideal k-stage pipeline needs k+n−1 cycles; 5+100−1=104 cycles.
500 cycles corresponds to executing every instruction through all five stages serially without overlap.
505 cycles incorrectly adds a full pipeline latency after every instruction.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Computer Organization and Architecture; instruction pipelining and throughput; Patterson and Hennessy, Computer Organization and Design, pipelined datapaths.

questions.stem: In cycle-stealing Direct Memory Access, how does the DMA controller typically obtain the system bus?
options: It disables the CPU permanently for the entire I/O transfer
It takes individual bus cycles when required, temporarily delaying CPU memory access
It copies data only through CPU registers and never becomes bus master
It interrupts the CPU after every byte and requires software to copy that byte
explanations: Cycle stealing does not permanently disable the CPU for the entire transfer.
Correct. The DMA controller temporarily takes individual bus cycles; CPU memory accesses may be delayed during those cycles.
DMA is specifically intended to transfer data without requiring the CPU to copy every word through its registers.
Per-byte software copying describes programmed I/O rather than cycle-stealing DMA.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Computer Organization and Architecture; I/O interface and DMA mode; Patterson and Hennessy, Computer Organization and Design, I/O and DMA.

questions.stem: In a conventional PC-relative addressing mode, the effective address is formed by which operation?
options: Adding a sign-extended displacement to the program counter (or the architecture-defined next-PC base)
Multiplying the displacement by the contents of the stack pointer
Using the displacement as an absolute physical address without modification
Adding the contents of the accumulator to the memory data bus
explanations: Correct. PC-relative addressing adds a signed displacement to a program-counter base, with the precise base (current or next instruction) defined by the architecture.
The stack pointer is not the base register in PC-relative addressing.
An absolute address uses the address field directly; PC-relative mode applies a PC-based offset.
The accumulator and memory data bus do not define PC-relative effective-address calculation.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Computer Organization and Architecture; machine instructions and addressing modes; Patterson and Hennessy, Computer Organization and Design, addressing modes.

questions.subtopic: C recursion with a static local variable
questions.stem: Consider the C function `int f(int n){ static int x=0; if(n==0) return 0; x++; return f(n-1)+x; }`. What does `f(3)` return when called once in a fresh program execution?
explanations: The function increments x three times; each of the three returning stack frames adds the final static value 3, so the result is not 3.
Six would result if only two increments were added during unwinding.
Correct. x becomes 1, then 2, then 3 before the base case returns; each of the three pending calls adds 3, giving 9.
Twelve would require four additions of 3, but only three non-base invocations occur.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Programming and Data Structures; C functions, recursion and storage duration; ISO C draft N1570, storage duration and block-scope static objects; https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf

questions.stem: Which declaration defines `fp` as a pointer to a function taking two `int` arguments and returning an `int`?
explanations: This declares fp as a function returning a pointer to int, not as a pointer to a function.
Correct. Parentheses bind the `*` to fp, making fp a pointer to a function with the stated parameter and return types.
This is not a valid declaration of the required function pointer.
The placement of `*` in this form is invalid C declarator syntax.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Programming and Data Structures; C programming, declarators and function pointers; ISO C draft N1570, declarators; https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf

questions.stem: In C, `strncpy(dest, src, n)` is called with `src` containing at least n non-null characters. Which statement is correct about the resulting destination array?
options: It is guaranteed to end with a null character
It contains exactly n characters and is always a valid C string
It may contain no terminating null character within the first n bytes
The function appends a null character after byte n in all cases
explanations: A null terminator is not guaranteed when the source length is at least n.
The copied bytes need not include a terminator, so the result is not always a valid C string.
Correct. `strncpy` pads with null bytes only when the source is shorter than n; if at least n non-null characters are copied, no null terminator is appended within those n bytes.
The function does not automatically write an extra byte after the n-byte destination region.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Programming and Data Structures; C strings and standard library; ISO C draft N1570, §7.24.2.4 strncpy; https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf

questions.stem: A binary max-heap containing n elements is stored in an array. What is the worst-case time complexity of inserting one new key?
explanations: O(1) is the best case when the new key remains at the leaf, not the worst case.
Correct. After insertion at the next leaf position, the key may move up at most the height of the heap, which is O(log n).
O(n) is not required because the heap property can be restored by following one rootward path.
O(n log n) would be unnecessarily high; insertion does not rebuild the entire heap.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Programming and Data Structures; binary heaps; CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms, priority queues and heap operations.

questions.subtopic: Kahn's topological sorting and cycle detection
questions.stem: Kahn's algorithm for topological sorting of a directed graph removes zero-indegree vertices repeatedly. If fewer than V vertices are output, what can be concluded?
options: The graph is necessarily a complete directed graph
The graph contains at least one directed cycle
The graph is disconnected but acyclic
Every vertex has indegree exactly one
explanations: A complete directed graph is not the specific condition detected by Kahn's algorithm.
Correct. If fewer than V vertices can be removed, the remaining subgraph has no zero-indegree vertex and therefore contains a directed cycle.
Disconnected acyclic directed graphs can still have all vertices output in a topological order.
The algorithm does not imply that every vertex has indegree one.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Algorithms; graph traversal and topological sorting; CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms, topological sort.

questions.stem: A depth-first search is run once over every vertex of a graph represented by adjacency lists. What is its time complexity in terms of V vertices and E edges?
explanations: O(V²) is the usual bound for an adjacency-matrix scan, not adjacency lists.
Correct. Each vertex is visited once and each adjacency-list edge is examined a constant number of times, giving O(V+E).
Sorting edges is not part of standard DFS.
O(VE) overstates the work for adjacency-list DFS.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Algorithms; graph traversals and complexity analysis; CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms, depth-first search.

questions.stem: Which complexity statement is correct for in-place heapsort on an array of n elements?
options: Worst-case O(n log n) time and O(1) auxiliary array space
Worst-case O(n²) time and O(log n) auxiliary array space
Worst-case O(n log n) time and O(n) auxiliary array space
Worst-case O(log n) time and O(1) auxiliary array space
explanations: Correct. Building a heap takes O(n), and n extract operations take O(n log n); the in-place array implementation uses O(1) auxiliary space.
O(n²) is not the worst-case running time of heapsort.
An additional O(n) array is not required by in-place heapsort.
O(log n) is too small for sorting n arbitrary keys under the comparison model.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Algorithms; sorting and best/worst-case time/space analysis; CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms, heapsort.

questions.stem: A dynamic array doubles its capacity whenever an append would exceed the current capacity. Starting with capacity 1, what is the amortised time complexity per append over a long sequence of n appends?
explanations: O(log n) is the number of resizing events, not the amortised cost per append.
O(n) describes the cost of a single resize at large capacity, not the amortised cost per append.
Correct. Most appends cost O(1); the total copying work across geometric capacity doublings is O(n), so the amortised cost per append is O(1).
O(n log n) overcounts the total copying work because capacities grow geometrically.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Algorithms; amortised analysis and dynamic data structures; CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms, aggregate and accounting methods.

questions.stem: How can one decide whether the language accepted by a finite DFA is empty?
options: Check whether every state is accepting
Perform graph reachability from the start state and test whether any accepting state is reachable
Count the number of transitions and compare it with the number of states
Minimise the DFA and inspect whether it has exactly one state
explanations: A DFA can accept a non-empty language even if some states are non-accepting; the test is reachability of an accepting state.
Correct. The accepted language is non-empty exactly when at least one accepting state is reachable from the initial state.
The raw number of transitions does not determine whether an accepting state can be reached.
A one-state minimal DFA may accept either the empty language or all strings depending on its accepting status; minimisation alone is not the test.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Theory of Computation; finite automata and decidability; Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation, decision problems for regular languages.

questions.stem: A standard way to decide whether two complete DFAs accept exactly the same language is to construct a product automaton for their symmetric difference. What must be tested in that product automaton?
options: Whether it has any reachable accepting state where exactly one component state is accepting
Whether both initial states are accepting
Whether every product state has two outgoing transitions
Whether the two DFAs have the same number of states
explanations: Correct. The symmetric-difference automaton accepts strings accepted by exactly one DFA; the languages are equivalent precisely when no accepting product state is reachable.
Initial-state acceptance alone cannot establish equivalence for all strings.
The number of outgoing transitions depends on the alphabet and completeness; it is not the equivalence criterion.
Equivalent DFAs may have different numbers of states before minimisation.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Theory of Computation; finite automata and language equivalence; Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation, closure and decision properties of regular languages.

questions.stem: An NFA has n states. Under the standard subset construction, what is the maximum possible number of states in an equivalent DFA before minimisation?
explanations: The construction can require more states than n because each DFA state represents a subset of NFA states.
n² is not the general upper bound for the subset construction.
2n is not the number of all subsets of an n-element state set.
Correct. An n-state NFA has 2ⁿ possible subsets of states, so the constructed DFA has at most 2ⁿ states.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Theory of Computation; finite automata and NFA-to-DFA conversion; Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation, subset construction.
